questions.q: Which shower has the fastest meteors, and which comet is its parent?
questions.do: Look at the speeds on the shower buttons in The next showers, or at the top bar of the energy chart in A grain with a bullet's punch.

questions.q: A Leonid is about 3.5 times faster than a Draconid. How much more energy does a 1 g Leonid grain carry?
questions.do: Read the bars for Leonids and Draconids in the A grain with a bullet's punch chart.
questions.a: Leonid: 2.49 MJ (like 594 g of TNT). Draconid: 0.20 MJ (48 g of TNT). That is about 12 times more, because energy grows with the square of speed: 3.5² ≈ 12.

questions.q: The page says it predicts each shower's date from the parent's orbit alone. How close is its prediction for the Perseids?
questions.do: Click the Perseids button. Read Closest to Earth's orbit, Predicted date, Observed peak and Difference under Why on this date?
questions.a: Comet Swift–Tuttle's orbit passes only 0.013 AU from Earth's. Predicted 12 Aug, observed 13 Aug: about 1 day off. Earth reaches that same point in its orbit on the same date every year.

questions.q: Why does Halley's Comet give us two showers a year, the Eta Aquariids in May and the Orionids in October?
questions.do: Click Eta Aquariids, then Orionids. Read the parent and the note under Why on this date? for each, and look at the orbit picture.
questions.a: Both come from Halley's Comet. Its dust is spread along its whole orbit, and Earth passes near that orbit at two places: once in May and once in October, on the other side of the orbit.

questions.q: Which shower has one of the oldest records, and in which year was it recorded?
questions.do: Click the Lyrids button and read the note under Why on this date?
questions.a: The Lyrids were recorded in China in 687 BCE, among the oldest shower records. Their parent is Comet Thatcher (C/1861 G1).
